plan.contextChunk: This figure contains two side-by-side circular diagrams, labeled (a) Sub-critical mass and (b) Critical mass, contrasting how sample size determines whether a nuclear fission chain reaction can become self-sustaining. In panel (a), a small blue circle contains a sparse arrangement of gold starburst symbols representing individual fission events, and the majority of the black arrows representing emitted neutrons point outward beyond the boundary of the circle, indicating that most neutrons escape the material without inducing further fissions; a single incoming neutron from the upper left initiates the limited sequence. In panel (b), a significantly larger blue circle is densely populated with many more fission-event starbursts, and the neutron arrows predominantly stay within the boundary and terminate at other fission sites, demonstrating that neutrons are captured and productive rather than lost; only a few arrows exit the periphery, and again one initiating neutron enters from the upper left. The visual contrast in circle size and in the fraction of escaping versus captured neutrons directly encodes the critical threshold: below the critical mass, neutron leakage prevents a sustained reaction, while at or above it, each fission event generates enough captured neutrons to propagate the chain indefinitely. This figure introduces the concept of critical mass as the minimum quantity of fissile material at which the rate of neutron production equals the combined rate of neutron absorption and escape, enabling a self-sustaining chain reaction.

interactionPlan.concept: Critical mass is the minimum size of fissile material needed for emitted neutrons to be captured often enough to sustain a nuclear fission chain reaction instead of escaping.

interactions.label: Mass case
interactions.teaches: Comparing the two cases shows that the larger sample loses a smaller fraction of neutrons at the surface, so more neutrons remain available to trigger additional fissions

interactions.label: Animate neutron cascade
interactions.teaches: A self-sustaining chain reaction grows because each fission releases neutrons that trigger multiple later fissions, producing a cascade across the critical mass

interactions.label: Fissile material mass
interactions.teaches: As the mass and radius increase, the surface leakage fraction falls; near the critical threshold, enough neutrons are retained for the chain reaction to continue

demo_steps.title: Start below the threshold
demo_steps.narration: In the sub-critical sample, the circle is small and most neutron arrows leave the material before hitting another nucleus. The chain reaction dies out because neutron escape exceeds productive neutron capture.

demo_steps.title: Increase the fissile mass
demo_steps.narration: Move the mass slider upward: the blue sample grows, and fewer neutron paths reach the boundary before another fission site. The decreasing escape fraction is the geometric reason a larger sample can sustain a reaction.

demo_steps.title: Reach critical mass
demo_steps.narration: At the critical threshold, neutron production balances neutron loss by escape and absorption. The diagram now emphasizes many internal neutron paths that connect one fission event to the next.

demo_steps.title: Watch the cascade
demo_steps.narration: Play the cascade animation in the critical mass: one incoming neutron triggers fission, then the next generations spread as 2, 4, and 8 events. This shows how retained neutrons make the reaction self-sustaining.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Critical mass is reached when the sample is large enough that enough neutrons stay inside to cause at least one further fission per fission event on average.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Recreate the original as two clean side-by-side circular panels on a white background, with bold titles above and panel labels below. Use translucent lavender-blue filled circles for fissile material, with the critical circle much larger than the sub-critical circle. Use gold/yellow starburst shapes with bright centers for fission events. Use thick black arrows for neutron paths: in the sub-critical panel, emphasize outward arrows crossing the circle boundary; in the critical panel, emphasize arrows connecting starbursts inside the circle with only a few escaping. The toggle should highlight or isolate the selected panel and display escape-versus-captured annotations. The slider should smoothly scale the circle and update the density of fission sites and the visible escape fraction, with a clear marker at the critical threshold. The animation should begin with the pale gray incoming neutron at the upper left of the critical mass and then reveal successive generations of starbursts and arrows across the large circle.

authoredContext:
Material that can sustain a nuclear fission chain reaction is said to be fissile or fissionable . (Technically, fissile material can undergo fission with neutrons of any energy, whereas fissionable material requires high-energy neutrons.) Nuclear fission becomes self-sustaining when the number of neutrons produced by fission equals or exceeds the number of neutrons absorbed by splitting nuclei plus the number that escape into the surroundings. The amount of a fissionable material that will support a self-sustaining chain reaction is a critical mass . An amount of fissionable material that cannot sustain a chain reaction is a subcritical mass . An amount of material in which there is an increasing rate of fission is known as a supercritical mass . The critical mass depends on the type of material: its purity, the temperature, the shape of the sample, and how the neutron reactions are controlled ( ).

Neutrons produced by nuclear reactions move too fast to cause fission (refer back to ). They must first be slowed to be absorbed by the fuel and produce additional nuclear reactions. A nuclear moderator is a substance that slows the neutrons to a speed that is low enough to cause fission. Early reactors used high-purity graphite as a moderator. Modern reactors in the US exclusively use heavy water ( 1 2 H 2 O ) or light water (ordinary H 2 O), whereas some reactors in other countries use other materials, such as carbon dioxide, beryllium, or graphite.

(a) In a subcritical mass, the fissile material is too small and allows too many neutrons to escape the material, so a chain reaction does not occur. (b) In a critical mass, a large enough number of neutrons in the fissile material induce fission to create a chain reaction.

The images are shown and labeled “a,” “b” and “c.” Image a, labeled “Sub-critical mass,” shows a blue circle background with a white sphere near the outer, top, left edge of the circle. A downward, right-facing arrow indicates that the white sphere enters the circle. Seven small, yellow starbursts are drawn in the blue circle and each has an arrow facing from it to outside the circle, in seemingly random directions. Image b, labeled “Critical mass,” shows a blue circle background with a white sphere near the outer, top, left edge of the circle. A downward, right-facing arrow indicates that the white sphere enters the circle. Seventeen small, yellow starbursts are drawn in the blue circle and each has an arrow facing from it to outside the circle, in seemingly random directions. Image c, labeled “Critical mass from neutron deflection,” shows a blue circle background, lying in a larger purple circle, with a white sphere near the outer, top, left edge of the purple circle. A downward, right-facing arrow indicates that the white sphere enters both of the circles. Thirteen small, yellow starbursts are drawn in the blue circle and each has an arrow facing from it to outside the blue circle, and a couple outside of the purple circle, in seemingly random directions.

An atomic bomb ( ) contains several pounds of fissionable material, 92 235 U or 94 239 Pu , a source of neutrons, and an explosive device for compressing it quickly into a small volume. When fissionable material is in small pieces, the proportion of neutrons that escape through the relatively large surface area is great, and a chain reaction does not take place. When the small pieces of fissionable material are brought together quickly to form a body with a mass larger than the critical mass, the relative number of escaping neutrons decreases, and a chain reaction and explosion result.

discrepancies: the black neutron arrows are substantially thicker and more visually dominant than in the source, making both panels look more crowded and maze-like
several arrow paths and fission-burst positions differ from the source, especially in the sub-critical panel where the original has more separated escape arrows rather than overlapping zig-zag paths
the generated figure is displayed much smaller alongside a large UI panel, so the default state is less like a direct static replacement for the source image
the critical-mass panel has slightly fewer and more uniformly sized fission bursts than the source, which has a denser, more varied distribution across the large circle
evaluation.notes: The two-circle comparison, labels, incoming neutrons, fission bursts, and neutron arrows are all recognizable and conceptually correct, but the arrows are over-scaled and the layout is less faithful as a static drop-in because of the prominent side controls.
action_items: Reduce the neutron arrow stroke width and arrowhead size so the arrows match the lighter, less cluttered appearance of the source.
Adjust arrow start/end points to more closely match the source paths, with more arrows visibly escaping the small sub-critical mass and less overlap between arrows.
Tune the fission-burst counts and positions, especially in the critical-mass panel, to better match the source distribution.
Make the default layout prioritize the figure more strongly, for example by using a more compact or collapsible control panel.
